terms.definition: Any value computed from the observations in a sample, such as their mean, their standard deviation, or the proportion of them above a cut-point. Because the sample was one of many that could have been drawn, a statistic is a quantity that would come out differently on a repeat.

A fixed numerical property of the whole population, such as its mean or its standard deviation. A parameter is one definite number that nobody has measured; a statistic computed from a sample is an estimate of it.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-010 defines a model parameter as a model quantity held fixed during one run and free to change between runs or calibrations. That is a setting the modeller chooses. The statistical sense used here is the opposite in one respect: a population parameter is a fact about the world that is fixed whether anyone knows it or not, and the whole point of a sample is to estimate it. Both senses are standard and the surrounding context decides which is meant; this lesson always means the population quantity.

terms.definition: The complete group a study means to describe, as opposed to the sample it actually measured. In this lesson the population has numerical properties of its own, including a mean and a standard deviation, and the sample's job is to estimate them.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-005 defines the target population as the whole group a study is meant to describe, as distinct from the group it enrolled, and this lesson keeps that meaning unchanged. What it adds is that the population has a mean and a standard deviation of its own, which are the quantities a sample mean and sample standard deviation estimate. The earlier lesson's point still governs everything here: a sample can at best speak for the frame it was drawn from, and no standard error repairs a frame that missed the intended population.

terms.definition: A value computed from a sample and offered as a stand-in for an unknown population quantity. Calling a number an estimate commits you to saying how far off it might be, which is what the standard error is for.

The differences between results computed from different samples drawn the same way from the same population. It arises because each sample contains different individuals, and it is present even when every step of the study was carried out correctly.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-008 defines random error as unpredictable variation across repetitions that contributes imprecision rather than a systematic shift, and lists sampling variation as one of its components alongside unpredictable measurement variation. This lesson uses that same idea narrowed to the sampling component only: the variation produced by drawing different individuals, with measurement held fixed. The word error in the alias sampling error carries no suggestion of a mistake, and the orientation scene says so before the term is used.

terms.definition: The distribution of the values a statistic would take across repeated samples of a fixed size drawn from the same population. For a sample mean it is centred on the population mean and is narrower than the distribution of the individual observations.

The standard deviation of a statistic's sampling distribution, which is to say how much that statistic would move from one repeat of the study to the next. For a mean it equals the standard deviation of the data divided by the square root of the number of observations, and it carries the same unit as the data.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-006 defines measurement error as the difference between a measured value and a reference value, which is the sense in which a mis-calibrated meter produces an error. A standard error contains the same word and reports something else entirely: how far a correctly computed statistic would move if the study were repeated on different people. No measurement is wrong when a standard error is large. The orientation scene names this collision before the term is first used and keeps both senses available.

terms.definition: The square root of the variance, returning the spread of a set of values to the unit of the data. Read it as roughly how far a typical observation sits from the mean. In this lesson it always describes individuals, and it is the input the standard error is computed from.

alignment.note: PREM-STA-003 owns this term and this lesson keeps its meaning exactly. It is restated here only because the whole misconception scene turns on holding it apart from the standard error, and a learner needs both definitions in view at once to do that. Anything about how a standard deviation is computed from the data belongs to the earlier lesson.

terms.definition: How closely repeated attempts at the same quantity agree with one another. Applied to an estimate, it means how little the estimate would move if the study were repeated, which is what the standard error measures. Precision says nothing about whether the estimate is aimed at the right population.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-006 defines measurement precision as how closely replicate measured values agree under specified conditions, and warns that precision describes dispersion without establishing closeness to a reference. This lesson keeps that meaning and extends what is being replicated: instead of repeating a measurement on one thing, the repeat is the whole study on a fresh sample. The earlier lesson's warning carries across intact, and the clinical wrap-up restates it as the point that a larger sample buys precision and nothing else.

terms.definition: The result that as the sample size grows, the sampling distribution of the mean becomes approximately normal whatever the shape of the population, is centred at the population mean, and has a standard deviation approaching the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. It is a statement about averages and says nothing about the individual observations.
